source_refs.note: Book p. 223: 12.2.2 lim (sqrt(x+a) - sqrt(a))/x = 1/(2 sqrt(a)) by rationalizing the numerator; Example 1 (i), (ii).

items.title: 12.2.2 Lim_{x->0} (sqrt(x+a) - sqrt(a))/x = 1/(2 sqrt(a)) where n is an integer and a > 0.

blocks.text: The heading of this section states the result "\(\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{\sqrt{x+a}-\sqrt{a}}{x} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{a}}\) where \(n\) is an integer and \(a > 0\)".

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The heading prints "where \(n\) is an integer and \(a > 0\)", but there is no \(n\) in this limit (the phrase is carried over from 12.2.1). The only condition is \(a > 0\). The arrow under "Lim" in the heading is also misprinted; it should read \(x \to 0\).

blocks.text_alt: limit as x approaches 0 of (square root of x plus a, minus square root of a) over x equals 1 over 2 times square root of a

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Substituting \(x = 0\) gives \(\frac{\sqrt{a}-\sqrt{a}}{0} = \frac{0}{0}\). Here there is no polynomial to factorize: the trouble comes from the square roots. The tool for square roots is rationalization.
By substituting \(x = 0\), we have \(\left(\frac{0}{0}\right)\) form, so rationalizing the numerator:

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Rationalizing means multiplying the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate \(\sqrt{x+a}+\sqrt{a}\). This is multiplying by 1, so the value does not change. It works because of
\[(A-B)(A+B) = A^{2}-B^{2}\]
\[(\sqrt{x+a}-\sqrt{a})(\sqrt{x+a}+\sqrt{a}) = (x+a) - a = x\]
The square roots disappear from the numerator and an \(x\) appears that cancels with the \(x\) below.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
In these two lines the book drops the factor \(x\) of the denominator. After multiplying, the denominator is \(x(\sqrt{x+a}+\sqrt{a})\), so the lines should read:
\[\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{x+a-a}{x\left(\sqrt{x+a}+\sqrt{a}\right)}\]
\[= \lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{x}{x\left(\sqrt{x+a}+\sqrt{a}\right)}\]
Cancelling \(x\) then gives the book's next line, and the final result \(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{a}}\) is correct.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why may we cancel \(x\)? Because \(x \to 0\) means \(x \ne 0\).
After cancelling, the denominator \(\sqrt{x+a}+\sqrt{a}\) equals \(2\sqrt{a} \ne 0\) at \(x = 0\) (since \(a > 0\)), so substitution works.
An example of our own: \(\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{\sqrt{x+4}-2}{x} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{4}} = \frac{1}{4}\) (here \(a = 4\), \(\sqrt{4} = 2\)).

blocks.title: Example 1
steps:
Given: (i) \(\frac{x^{2}-1}{x^{2}-x}\) as \(x \to 1\); (ii) \(\frac{x-3}{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{3}}\) as \(x \to 3\).
To find: both limits.
Method: substitution gives \(\frac{0}{0}\) in both parts. In (i) we factorize and cancel the common factor \((x-1)\). In (ii) we write \(x - 3\) as a difference of squares of \(\sqrt{x}\) and \(\sqrt{3}\) and cancel \((\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{3})\).

(i) Step 1: Try substitution
\[\dfrac{1^{2}-1}{1^{2}-1} = \dfrac{0}{0}\]
Why: substitution always comes first. It gives the \(\left(\frac{0}{0}\right)\) form, so we must simplify.

(i) Step 2: Factorize and cancel
\[\lim_{x\to 1}\dfrac{x^{2}-1}{x^{2}-x} = \lim_{x\to 1}\dfrac{(x-1)(x+1)}{x(x-1)}\]
\[= \lim_{x\to 1}\dfrac{x+1}{x}\]
Why: \(x^{2}-1\) is a difference of squares and \(x^{2}-x\) has the common factor \(x\). The factor \((x-1)\) is zero at \(x = 1\); it is the cause of \(\frac{0}{0}\), and it is non-zero while \(x \to 1\), so it may be cancelled.

(i) Step 3: Substitute
\[\lim_{x\to 1}\dfrac{x+1}{x} = \dfrac{1+1}{1} = \dfrac{2}{1} = 2\]
Why: after cancelling, the denominator is no longer zero at \(x = 1\), so substitution now works.

(ii) Step 1: Try substitution
\[\dfrac{3-3}{\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{0}{0}\]
Why: again the \(\left(\frac{0}{0}\right)\) form, so we simplify.

(ii) Step 2: Write \(x - 3\) as a difference of squares
\[x - 3 = (\sqrt{x})^{2} - (\sqrt{3})^{2}\]
\[= (\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{3})(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{3})\]
Why: for \(x > 0\), \(x = (\sqrt{x})^{2}\) and \(3 = (\sqrt{3})^{2}\), so \(a^{2}-b^{2} = (a+b)(a-b)\) applies. This produces the factor in the denominator.

(ii) Step 3: Cancel and substitute
\[\lim_{x\to 3}\dfrac{x-3}{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{3}}\]
\[= \lim_{x\to 3}\dfrac{(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{3})(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{3})}{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{3}}\]
\[= \lim_{x\to 3}(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{3})\]
\[= \sqrt{3}+\sqrt{3} = 2\sqrt{3}\]
Why: \(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{3} \ne 0\) while \(x \to 3\) (\(x \ne 3\)), so it cancels; what is left is defined at \(x = 3\).

Check:
(i) Take \(x = 1.001\): \(\frac{x+1}{x} = \frac{2.001}{1.001} \approx 1.999\), close to 2.
(ii) The same answer comes from rationalizing instead: multiply up and down by \(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{3}\); the denominator becomes \(x - 3\), which cancels, leaving \(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{3} \to 2\sqrt{3}\).

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: When a square root causes \(\frac{0}{0}\), there are two routes: multiply by the conjugate (rationalize), or, as in Example 1 (ii), write the other factor as a difference of squares. Both give the same answer; choose the shorter one and show every line.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{\sqrt{x+a}-\sqrt{a}}{x} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{a}}\), \(a > 0\).
2. Square roots causing \(\frac{0}{0}\): rationalize with the conjugate, using \((A-B)(A+B) = A^{2}-B^{2}\).
3. Polynomials causing \(\frac{0}{0}\): factorize and cancel the factor that is zero at the point.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Multiplying only the numerator by the conjugate. Multiply the numerator and the denominator, otherwise the value changes.
2. Writing \(\sqrt{x+a} = \sqrt{x}+\sqrt{a}\). This is false: e.g. \(\sqrt{9+16} = 5\) but \(\sqrt{9}+\sqrt{16} = 7\).
3. Losing the \(x\) of the denominator after multiplying out, so nothing is left to cancel (as happens in the book's printed lines).
